parts.title: Part 2. Read the article and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
When Dilnoza finished school, she was not sure what to study at university. Her parents wanted her to become a doctor, but she was more interested in animals. Instead of choosing a course immediately, she decided to spend a year as a volunteer at the animal shelter in her city.

The shelter looks after around eighty dogs and cats that have lost their homes. Volunteers clean the rooms, prepare food and take the dogs for walks twice a day. At first, Dilnoza found the work tiring. 'I went home every evening with dirty clothes and sore feet,' she says. 'But after a few weeks I started to feel stronger, and I loved seeing the animals get healthier.'

The most difficult part of the job, she says, was not the physical work but saying goodbye. When a family adopts an animal, the volunteers are happy, but they also miss the animal they have cared for. Dilnoza remembers an old dog called Bars who waited almost a year for a new home. 'Everyone thought nobody would take him because of his age. Then a retired teacher came in and chose him immediately. I cried, but they were tears of joy.'

The year at the shelter helped Dilnoza make her decision. She has now started a degree in veterinary medicine. She still visits the shelter at weekends and encourages other young people to try volunteering before they choose a career. 'You learn what you really enjoy,' she says, 'and that is worth more than any test result.'

parts.title: Part 3. Choose the best heading for each paragraph. There are two headings you do not need.

headings.text: Plan your money from the start

paragraphs.text: At school, teachers tell you what to do and when. At university, you may have only fifteen hours of classes a week and a lot of free time. That freedom can be a trap. Successful students write a weekly timetable that includes reading, assignments and rest, and they treat study hours as seriously as lectures.

Many students receive their grant, or money from their parents, at the start of the month and have nothing left by the third week. Before you spend anything, write down your fixed costs: rent, transport and your phone. What is left is what you can really spend, and dividing it by four gives you a simple weekly limit.

Feeling lost in a difficult subject is normal, but waiting until the exam to admit it is not. Tutors have office hours exactly for this reason, and most universities also offer free writing or maths support. Students who use these services in the first months usually avoid much bigger problems later.

Late-night conversations and online series are part of student life, yet research shows that students who regularly get less than six hours a night remember less of what they study. Try to go to bed at roughly the same time each night, especially in the weeks before exams.

It is natural to spend time with people from your own group, because you see them every day. However, your neighbours in the dormitory or students from other faculties can introduce you to new ideas and even future job opportunities. A wider circle also helps when the people you study with are busy.

Moving to a new city can make even confident students homesick. A short call to your family every few days keeps you connected without stopping you from building a new life. Some students also find it helps to bring a few familiar things, such as photos or a favourite blanket.

parts.title: Part 4. Read the text and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
Teachers have long suspected that a good story sticks in the mind far longer than a list of facts, and cognitive scientists now have a fairly clear account of why. When we read a list, each item is stored more or less on its own, with few connections to anything else. A story, by contrast, links events through cause and effect: this happened because of that, and therefore something else followed. Each link acts as a retrieval cue, so that recalling one event tends to pull the next one with it.

Stories also engage emotion, and emotionally charged information is given priority by the brain. This is not simply a matter of excitement. Even mild curiosity, wanting to know what happens next, appears to prepare the brain to store new information, which may explain why students remember facts better when they are presented as answers to a question they have already started to wonder about.

None of this means that every lesson should be turned into a narrative. Critics point out that stories can be misleading precisely because they are memorable. A vivid anecdote about one patient who recovered after an unusual treatment may stay with us longer than the dull statistics showing that the treatment rarely works. In other words, the very features that make stories effective teaching tools also make them effective tools for spreading errors.

The practical lesson for learners is therefore a balanced one. Turning material into a story, by explaining to yourself why one event led to another or imagining how a historical figure might have felt, is a powerful way to remember it. But it should be combined with a habit of checking: asking whether the story fits the evidence, and whether a more boring explanation might be closer to the truth. Memorable and accurate are not the same thing, and good learners look for both.

parts.title: Part 2. Listen to a talk about a summer camp. Complete the notes with ONE word or a number.
parts.script: Hello everyone, and welcome to this information session about our summer English camp. The camp takes place in the Chimgan mountains, about ninety kilometres from Tashkent. This year it runs from the fifth of July to the eighteenth of July, so that's two weeks in total. Students between fourteen and seventeen can apply. Every morning there are four hours of lessons, and in the afternoons students choose activities such as hiking, photography or drama. On the last evening, each group performs a short play in English for the parents. The price includes accommodation, all meals and transport by bus from the city centre. Students sleep in wooden cabins, with six students in each cabin. Please remember that phones are allowed only in the evening, between seven and nine. To apply, fill in the form on our website and send a short video introducing yourself. The deadline for applications is the first of June. If you have any questions, you can call the office or speak to me after this session.

parts.title: Part 3. Listen to two students planning a presentation. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
Kamola: So, have you looked at the topic for our presentation? Renewable energy in Central Asia.
Timur: I have. I think we should focus on solar power. Uzbekistan has more than three hundred sunny days a year, so it's the obvious example.
Kamola: That's true, but the teacher said she wanted us to compare at least two sources of energy. If we only talk about solar, we'll lose marks.
Timur: Fair point. What about wind, then? I read that there are big wind farm projects in Karakalpakstan.
Kamola: Good, that gives us a contrast. I can find the figures on wind if you take solar.
Timur: Deal. How long does it need to be?
Kamola: Ten minutes, plus five minutes for questions. Honestly, it's the questions I'm worried about. Last time, the teacher asked about costs and nobody could answer.
Timur: Then let's prepare a slide on costs, even if we don't show it. If someone asks, we'll have the numbers ready.
Kamola: Smart. And who's going to speak first?
Timur: You should. You're more confident in front of people. I'll do the second half and the conclusion.
Kamola: All right, but you have to promise to practise. Last time you read everything from your notes.
Timur: I know, I know. Let's rehearse together on Thursday evening in the library.
Kamola: Thursday doesn't work for me, I've got my part-time job. What about Wednesday?
Timur: Wednesday's fine. Six o'clock?
Kamola: Perfect.

parts.title: Part 4. Listen to part of a lecture. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
Good afternoon. Today I want to look at a problem that most city dwellers have felt but few can name: the urban heat island. On a summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. The reasons are fairly well understood. Asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while buildings trap warm air and reduce the wind that would otherwise carry it away. Add the heat produced by cars and air conditioners, and you have a city that never really cools down.
Why does this matter? The obvious answer is comfort, but the more serious answer is health. Heat waves kill more people than most other kinds of extreme weather, and the victims are disproportionately elderly people living alone in top-floor flats. A city that stays hot at night denies their bodies the chance to recover.
The most popular solution is to plant trees, and trees certainly help, both by providing shade and by releasing moisture into the air. But I want to warn against seeing trees as a complete answer. A young tree takes years to grow a useful canopy, and in a dry climate it needs water that may be scarce. Some of the quickest gains, in fact, come from much less romantic measures: painting roofs in light colours so that they reflect sunlight, and replacing dark car parks with surfaces that let rain through.
Finally, there is a question of fairness. Research from several cities shows that wealthier districts tend to have more green space and are therefore cooler. Any serious plan has to start with the neighbourhoods that are hottest, not those whose residents complain the loudest. That, I would argue, is the real test of whether a city takes the problem seriously.

input.subject: Changes to the Sunday football club
input.body:
Dear members,

From next month, our Sunday football sessions will move from the city stadium to a new pitch on the edge of the city, and they will start at 8 a.m. instead of 10 a.m. The monthly membership fee will also rise slightly. We would like to hear what you think about these changes, and any ideas you have for the club.

Sardor Karimov, Club Manager
